questions.question: A 13B model in FP16 occupies 26 GB on an 80 GB A100 GPU. Single-request execution latency is 45 ms against a 200 ms latency SLO. Sustained traffic has grown from 8,000 QPS to 18,000 QPS, but a single replica tops out at 10,000 QPS. Which distribution strategy matches the constraint that is actually binding?
choices: Tensor parallelism across two GPUs, because splitting weight matrices is the standard technique to increase throughput regardless of whether the model fits on a single device
Horizontal replication, because the model fits in single-device memory and single-request latency satisfies the SLO, so only aggregate throughput capacity needs to scale
Pipeline parallelism across four stages, because stage-wise execution allows a single request to finish sooner and doubles per-device capacity
Disaggregated prefill and decode pools, because phase separation is required whenever traffic exceeds 10,000 QPS
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. Horizontal replication, because the model fits in single-device memory and single-request latency satisfies the SLO, so only aggregate throughput capacity needs to scale. The section's trigger taxonomy separates memory capacity, latency SLO, and throughput constraints. Here, memory is satisfied (26 GB < 80 GB) and latency is well within budget (45 ms < 200 ms). The only binding limit is aggregate throughput, making horizontal replication of independent stateless replicas the matched lever. Tensor parallelism (A) targets intra-layer execution latency or memory-fit issues, introducing unnecessary AllReduce communication without raising single-replica QPS when already compute-saturated. Pipeline parallelism (C) does not reduce single-request latency because a request must still traverse all stages sequentially. Disaggregation (D) addresses the compute-versus-bandwidth mismatch between prefill and decode phases rather than aggregate replica count.
questions.learning_objective: Classify a production serving bottleneck against the memory, throughput, and latency trigger framework to select the matching distribution strategy.

questions.question: A team spent \$12,000 training a recommendation model (1,000 GPU-hours at \$3/hr with a 3x engineering multiplier) and now serves it at 10,000 QPS for two years at \$10 per million queries. Using the chapter's cost-dominance framework, calculate the lifetime serving-to-training cost ratio and explain the resulting engineering investment trade-off between training-side and serving-side optimization.
questions.answer: Lifetime queries served are $10{,}000\text{ QPS} \times 86{,}400\text{ s/day} \times 730\text{ days} \approx 6.31 \times 10^{11}$ requests. At \$10 per million queries, the total lifetime serving cost is approximately \$6.31 million against the initial \$12,000 training cost—a serving-to-training ratio of roughly 525:1. Because operating expenses dominate by over two orders of magnitude, a 1% reduction in serving cost saves approximately \$63,100 over two years (\$31,550/year), whereas a 1% speedup in training saves only \$120 once. Consequently, ML systems engineering effort should be overwhelmingly directed toward serving-side optimizations—such as dynamic batching, KV-cache management, weight quantization, and efficient routing—once a model reaches production.
questions.learning_objective: Calculate the lifetime serving-to-training cost ratio for high-QPS production workloads and justify the strategic prioritization of serving-side optimizations.

questions.question: Why does a cluster infrastructure tuned for distributed training throughput generally make a poor production inference serving deployment?
choices: Training optimizes for aggregate batch throughput over hours and tolerates variance via checkpoint-based recovery, whereas serving strictly optimizes for P99 tail latency in milliseconds and requires seamless request-level failover
Training clusters use FP16/BF16 precision weights whereas inference serving clusters can only execute INT4 integer arithmetic
Training relies on AllReduce collective communication which is physically prohibited in inference serving networks
Training workloads require stateful memory retention across queries whereas inference serving is universally stateless
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. Training optimizes for aggregate batch throughput over hours and tolerates variance via checkpoint-based recovery, whereas serving strictly optimizes for P99 tail latency in milliseconds and requires seamless request-level failover. The fundamental inversion establishes six divergence dimensions between training and serving: objective (samples/hr vs. P99 tail latency), batch size (thousands vs. single-digits/dynamic), latency tolerance (hours vs. milliseconds), failure mode (restart from checkpoint vs. transparent real-time failover), workload predictability (deterministic iterations vs. stochastic arrival), and cost structure (one-time CapEx vs. compounding OpEx). Precision differences (B) are optimization choices, not architectural barriers. Collective operations like AllReduce (C) are actively used in tensor-parallel serving. Autoregressive inference with KV caching is stateful, making D incorrect.
questions.learning_objective: Contrast the operational and performance invariants of distributed training clusters with production inference serving architectures.

questions.question: An LLM service measures 70 ms of raw model compute on a single accelerator, but once deployed in a distributed serving stack under live traffic, the measured end-to-end latency rises to 95 ms. Given the serving tax decomposition $T_{\text{total}} = T_{\text{compute}} + T_{\text{network}} + T_{\text{serialization}} + T_{\text{coordination}} + T_{\text{queuing}}$, which diagnosis is most consistent with the observed 25 ms gap?
choices: The gap indicates model accuracy degradation, causing client applications to re-issue duplicate requests that inflate perceived server execution time
Distributing the model transformed the underlying matrix multiplication kernels from memory-bandwidth-bound to compute-bound, adding 25 ms of arithmetic time
The overhead is caused by frequent model checkpoint writes to distributed persistent storage during forward inference passes

The 25 ms gap represents the serving tax: network RPCs, tensor serialization/deserialization, load-balancer routing, coordination overhead, and queuing delays, which typically consume 10–30% of the total latency budget
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. The 25 ms gap represents the serving tax: network RPCs, tensor serialization/deserialization, load-balancer routing, coordination overhead, and queuing delays, which typically consume 10–30% of the total latency budget. The serving tax comprises non-compute latency components: network RTT (50–500 µs per hop), tensor serialization (especially large activation buffers), gateway routing, scheduler coordination, and queue wait time; here, $25\text{ ms} / 95\text{ ms} \approx 26.3\%$, falling squarely in the expected 10–30% range. Model accuracy (A) affects application logic but does not explain systems middleware overhead. Distribution adds communication overhead but does not change the arithmetic intensity of local GPU compute kernels (B). Checkpointing (C) is a training-state persistence mechanism never executed in the online inference latency path.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze end-to-end inference latency using the serving tax decomposition to identify non-compute systems overheads.

questions.question: Which sequence correctly orders the four tiers of the Serving Hierarchy from narrowest operational scope (single query) to broadest system-wide scope (entire infrastructure fleet)?
choices: Replica level -> Request level -> Service level -> Platform level
Platform level -> Service level -> Replica level -> Request level

Request level (tokenization, batch formation) -> Replica level (local KV cache, kernel execution) -> Service level (load balancing, autoscaling) -> Platform level (multi-tenant scheduling, resource isolation)
Request level -> Service level -> Replica level -> Platform level
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. Request level (tokenization, batch formation) -> Replica level (local KV cache, kernel execution) -> Service level (load balancing, autoscaling) -> Platform level (multi-tenant scheduling, resource isolation). The Serving Hierarchy organizes inference engineering into four distinct layers analogous to the computer memory hierarchy. The request level focuses on single-query lifecycle (preprocessing, prompt caching, token generation). The replica level governs single-instance throughput and efficiency (GPU kernel fusion, KV-cache layout, local scheduling). The service level coordinates multiple replicas of a single model (fleet load balancing, traffic routing, autoscaling). The platform level manages cross-service infrastructure (multi-tenancy, hardware allocation, cost governance). Inverting or swapping levels confuses local execution mechanics with fleet-wide orchestration.
questions.learning_objective: Identify and order the four tiers of the Serving Hierarchy according to their architectural scope and optimization focus.

questions.question: A team is designing a serving architecture for an interactive multi-turn conversational LLM where user prompt lengths vary from 50 to 2,000 tokens and generated outputs range from 30 to 3,000 tokens. Which configuration across the five architectural dimensions matches this workload's constraint profile?
choices: Static batching, pre-allocated contiguous memory, FCFS scheduling, single-GPU deployment, stateless routing
Feature-parallel batching, sharded embedding tables, priority-only scheduling, hybrid CPU-GPU topology, stateless routing
Continuous batching, paged KV-cache memory, preemptive/priority-aware scheduling, tensor-parallel topology, stateful sticky routing
Single-frame streaming, zero-copy buffer memory, FCFS scheduling, edge topology, stateless routing
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. Continuous batching, paged KV-cache memory, preemptive/priority-aware scheduling, tensor-parallel topology, stateful sticky routing. Autoregressive LLM generation has high output-length variance (100x range), making continuous batching necessary to reclaim slots immediately as short requests finish; paged memory (e.g., PagedAttention) prevents the 60–80% memory waste of maximum-length pre-allocation; preemption prevents rare 3,000-token generations from causing head-of-line blocking; tensor parallelism shards large weights across GPUs; and multi-turn KV-cache reuse requires sticky routing to preserve cache locality. Static batching with pre-allocation (A) fits fixed-shape vision models. Feature-parallel batching with sharded tables (B) matches recommendation embeddings. Streaming without batching (D) fits real-time audio.
questions.learning_objective: Map the constraint profile of an autoregressive LLM workload onto the five core serving architecture dimensions.

questions.question: Explain why autoregressive LLM serving with persistent multi-turn conversations is classified as stateful rather than stateless, and describe the cascading architectural consequences for load balancing, scale-down autoscaling, and replica failure recovery.
questions.answer: Autoregressive serving is stateful because the KV cache accumulated during a multi-turn conversation resides in a specific replica's GPU memory; recreating this state on another node requires re-running the entire conversation history through the compute-intensive prefill phase. This statefulness triggers three major architectural constraints: (1) Load balancing requires sticky routing (e.g., via consistent hashing) to direct subsequent turns of a session to the replica holding its cached KV state; (2) Autoscaling down cannot immediately terminate instances, but must gracefully drain active sessions over several minutes to avoid breaking user conversations; and (3) Failure recovery is expensive, as a replica crash forces either user-visible latency spikes (recomputing full prefill context from scratch) or total loss of session context.
questions.learning_objective: Explain the mechanisms of statefulness in LLM inference and analyze its consequences for routing, draining, and fault tolerance.

questions.question: Explain why First-Come, First-Served (FCFS) scheduling causes severe head-of-line blocking in an LLM service with high output-length variance (50 to 4,000 tokens), whereas FCFS is entirely satisfactory for a ResNet-50 vision service.
questions.answer: Under FCFS with wide output-length variance (an 80x spread), a single 4,000-token generation admitted to a batch slot monopolizes that slot for thousands of decode iterations (~20 ms each $\approx 80\text{ s}$). Short 50-token requests queued behind it suffer massive queueing delay, collapsing their P99 latency. Preemptive scheduling resolves this by swapping the long request's KV state to host memory or pausing it when it exceeds a threshold, allowing short requests to complete in ~1 s. In contrast, ResNet-50 processes fixed 224x224 images where every forward pass takes virtually identical execution time (deterministic runtime with zero output variance). Because service time is uniform, FCFS creates no head-of-line distortion and avoids the memory-swapping complexity of preemption.
questions.learning_objective: Evaluate how output execution variance dictates the choice between FCFS and preemptive scheduling policies.

questions.question: A serving engine statically pre-allocates contiguous KV-cache memory for each admitted request based on the model's maximum sequence limit of 4,096 tokens. Under a production distribution where 90% of requests generate only 200–500 tokens, what is the primary concurrency bottleneck?
choices: Pre-allocation maximizes GPU memory bandwidth utilization by forcing all memory reads to be physically contiguous in HBM
Pre-allocation eliminates external memory fragmentation, making dynamic batch insertion 10x faster than paged attention
Pre-allocation shifts the decode phase from memory-bandwidth-bound to compute-bound by standardizing tensor shapes

Pre-allocation wastes 88–95% of allocated KV memory on ungenerated tokens, artificially capping concurrent batch capacity; paged KV memory eliminates this internal fragmentation, enabling 2–4x higher concurrency on identical hardware
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. Pre-allocation wastes 88–95% of allocated KV memory on ungenerated tokens, artificially capping concurrent batch capacity; paged KV memory eliminates this internal fragmentation, enabling 2–4x higher concurrency on identical hardware. Reserving 4,096 tokens when requests use only 200–500 tokens leaves the vast majority of reserved HBM allocated but unused (internal fragmentation). Furthermore, contiguous memory requirements cause external fragmentation as variable-length requests arrive and depart. Paged memory (e.g., PagedAttention) allocates fixed-size blocks (e.g., 16 tokens) on demand via a virtual block table, recovering 60–80% of wasted memory and translating directly into 2–4x higher concurrent request capacity. Pre-allocation does not make decode compute-bound (C), nor does it improve available concurrency (B, C).
questions.learning_objective: Quantify the memory waste of static KV pre-allocation and explain how paged memory management multiplies concurrent serving capacity.

questions.question: A production recommendation system evaluates thousands of candidate items per user request across embedding tables totaling over 10 TB of sparse features, followed by a lightweight dense ranking MLP. Which architectural design matches this system's bottleneck profile?
choices: Feature-parallel batching with sharded embedding tables, priority-aware scheduling, hybrid CPU-GPU topology, and stateless request routing
Continuous batching with paged KV memory, preemptive scheduling, tensor-parallel GPU topology, and stateful sticky routing
Static batching with pre-allocated GPU memory, FCFS scheduling, single-GPU replicas, and stateful routing
Streaming single-item inference with zero batching, CPU-only execution, and edge caching
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. Feature-parallel batching with sharded embedding tables, priority-aware scheduling, hybrid CPU-GPU topology, and stateless request routing. Recommendation workloads are dominated by sparse memory lookups across multi-terabyte embedding tables that exceed single-GPU HBM capacity. The matched architecture shards embedding tables across host CPU memory / SSD pools (or dedicated memory nodes) and uses feature-parallel batching to aggregate lookups by feature type; retrieved embeddings are then fed to GPU workers for dense MLP ranking (hybrid topology). The requests are stateless, so routing does not require session stickiness. Continuous batching and paged KV cache (B) are specific to autoregressive LLM decoding. Single-GPU static batching (C) cannot accommodate 10 TB of tables.
questions.learning_objective: Identify the optimal serving architecture configuration across all five dimensions for embedding-dominated recommendation systems.

questions.question: Why do autoregressive LLM decode workloads benefit from much larger effective batch sizes than vision-inference workloads running on the same GPU hardware?
choices: Vision models stop benefiting from batching as soon as requests are distributed across multiple GPU replicas

LLM decode is memory-bandwidth-bound on loading model weights from HBM, so each additional request in the batch reuses weights already streamed to on-chip SRAM and amortizes the memory traffic across more tokens
LLM decode is compute-bound while vision inference is memory-bandwidth-bound, so larger LLM batches reduce the arithmetic backlog faster
Larger LLM batches compress the per-request KV cache by sharing attention keys across unrelated sequences
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. LLM decode is memory-bandwidth-bound on loading model weights from HBM, so each additional request in the batch reuses weights already streamed to on-chip SRAM and amortizes the memory traffic across more tokens. In autoregressive decode, generating a single token requires streaming tens of gigabytes of model weights from HBM to compute only a single vector-matrix product (arithmetic intensity $\approx 1\text{ FLOP/byte}$, severely memory-bandwidth-bound). Batching $B$ requests streams the exact same weights once but performs $B$ vector-matrix products (matrix-matrix multiplication), raising arithmetic intensity linearly with $B$ toward the compute roofline. Vision inference (e.g., ResNet/ViT) operates on dense tensors with high arithmetic intensity even at small batches, reaching compute saturation at modest batch sizes ($B=16\text{--}32$). Decode is not compute-bound (C), nor can unrelated sequences share KV caches (D).
questions.learning_objective: Explain the physical mechanism behind the batching efficiency curve for memory-bandwidth-bound LLM decode versus compute-bound vision inference.

questions.question: An inference service receives an arrival rate of $\lambda = 1{,}000$ requests per second with an end-to-end latency SLO of $T_{\text{lat}} = 100$ ms. Apply Little's Law to derive the steady-state concurrency requirement, and explain why provisioning replica throughput to exactly match the mean arrival rate results in severe SLO violations.
questions.answer: Little's Law states $L = \lambda W$, so the steady-state concurrency is $Q_{\text{req}} = 1{,}000\,\text{req/s} \times 0.1\,\text{s} = 100$ requests in flight simultaneously. Provisioning aggregate replica throughput to match exactly the mean arrival rate ($1{,}000\text{ req/s}$) operates the system at utilization $\rho = 1.0$. Queueing theory establishes that as $\rho \to 1$, mean queue length and waiting time grow non-linearly as $1/(1-\rho)$ (the queueing cliff). Under stochastic, bursty arrival patterns, any temporary arrival surge forces requests to queue indefinitely, causing catastrophic P99 and P99.9 latency spikes that violate the 100 ms SLO. Systems planners must provision for peak arrival rates plus queueing headroom, typically targeting 60–75% average utilization so bursts decay rapidly without breaching latency bounds.
questions.learning_objective: Apply Little's Law to calculate steady-state inference concurrency and explain the necessity of queueing headroom against utilization saturation.

questions.question: In dynamic batching for vision models, what is the consequence of configuring a larger maximum batch formation wait window (e.g., increasing timeout from 5 ms to 20 ms)?
choices: It strictly decreases end-to-end response latency by eliminating kernel launch overheads on the accelerator
It shifts the execution model from batch inference to real-time streaming inference
It guarantees that every formed batch will reach the configured maximum batch size regardless of traffic arrival rate
It allows larger batches to accumulate, increasing GPU throughput and hardware utilization, but consumes latency headroom and increases response time for early-arriving requests
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. It allows larger batches to accumulate, increasing GPU throughput and hardware utilization, but consumes latency headroom and increases response time for early-arriving requests. Dynamic batching trades latency headroom for batching efficiency. An early-arriving request must wait in the accumulation buffer for either the batch to fill or the timeout window to expire. Lengthening the wait window allows higher batch sizes during moderate traffic, amortizing fixed compute overheads and raising QPS capacity, but directly adds up to the full timeout duration to the queuing delay of the first request in the batch. It does not reduce latency (A), nor does it guarantee full batches if traffic is very sparse (C).
questions.learning_objective: Analyze the fundamental trade-off between batch formation delay, accelerator utilization, and tail latency in dynamic batching.

questions.question: A serving engine is processing four active requests with output lengths of 50, 100, 150, and 200 tokens at 20 ms per decode iteration. How does continuous batching reduce average latency and improve utilization compared to traditional static batching?
choices: Continuous batching parallelizes the autoregressive token generation of the 200-token request across all four batch slots

Continuous batching allows the 50-token request to depart at iteration 50 (1,000 ms) and immediately admits a new request into the freed slot, whereas traditional batching forces all requests to wait 200 iterations (4,000 ms) until the longest request completes
Continuous batching stops computing attention for shorter sequences while continuing to charge them for full batch latency
Continuous batching eliminates the need for KV caches, allowing all sequences to share intermediate activations
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. Continuous batching allows the 50-token request to depart at iteration 50 (1,000 ms) and immediately admits a new request into the freed slot, whereas traditional batching forces all requests to wait 200 iterations (4,000 ms) until the longest request completes. Traditional batching operates at the granularity of the entire batch; all sequences remain locked in the batch until the maximum sequence length $S_{\text{max}}$ completes, resulting in a waste ratio $W = 1 - \bar{S}/S_{\text{max}} = 1 - 125/200 = 37.5\%$. Continuous (iteration-level) batching schedules at the granularity of individual decode iterations: as soon as sequence 1 finishes at iteration 50, its slot is reclaimed, its response is returned to the user in 1.0 s instead of 4.0 s, and a new waiting request is inserted without pausing execution. Autoregressive token dependencies cannot be parallelized across slots (A).
questions.learning_objective: Analyze how continuous batching's iteration-level slot reclamation reduces response latency and eliminates variable-length batch waste.

questions.question: A real-time speech recognition service processes 20 ms audio frames under a strict 100 ms total end-to-end latency budget, with new frames arriving every 20 ms. Which batching strategy is appropriate for this workload?
choices: Static batching at size 64, because uniform 20 ms frames guarantee optimal GPU arithmetic efficiency regardless of arrival timing
Feature-parallel batching, because audio spectrograms require distributed embedding lookups similar to recommendation models
Streaming inference with minimal or zero batch accumulation, because any batch formation wait directly consumes the remaining latency margin required for model compute and audio output
Continuous batching with paged memory, because audio frames exhibit high output length variance
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. Streaming inference with minimal or zero batch accumulation, because any batch formation wait directly consumes the remaining latency margin required for model compute and audio output. When inter-frame arrival cadence matches the physical time step (20 ms) and the total latency budget is tight (100 ms), batch accumulation delay (e.g., waiting 60 ms to collect 4 frames) leaves only 40 ms for compute, network transmission, and decoding. In hard real-time streaming, latency deadline compliance strictly dominates accelerator utilization efficiency; frames must be processed as soon as they arrive (or in micro-windows of 1–2 frames). Static batching (A) causes immediate deadline violations. Audio signals are dense continuous features, not sparse recommendation embeddings (B).
questions.learning_objective: Select the appropriate batching strategy under hard real-time deadline constraints, recognizing when accumulation delays violate latency budgets.

questions.question: What is the correct sequential execution flow of data dependencies in a feature-parallel recommendation serving pipeline?
choices: Request routing to embedding shards -> Shard batch accumulation over time window -> Sparse embedding lookup -> Dense feature interaction processing -> Ranking MLP final scoring
Ranking MLP final scoring -> Dense feature interaction processing -> Sparse embedding lookup -> Shard batch accumulation -> Request routing
Dense feature interaction processing -> Ranking MLP final scoring -> Shard batch accumulation -> Sparse embedding lookup
Sparse embedding lookup -> Request routing -> Ranking MLP final scoring -> Dense feature interaction processing
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. Request routing to embedding shards -> Shard batch accumulation over time window -> Sparse embedding lookup -> Dense feature interaction processing -> Ranking MLP final scoring. The dataflow reflects strict physical dependencies: incoming queries must first be routed to the specific memory shards holding the relevant embedding tables; each shard accumulates lookups over a brief micro-window to amortize memory bus transactions; sparse embedding vectors are retrieved and gathered across shards; the retrieved vectors are combined with dense features; and finally the dense ranking MLP scores candidate items. Executing ranking before embedding retrieval (B, C) violates fundamental data dependencies.
questions.learning_objective: Sequence the execution phases of a feature-parallel recommendation serving pipeline based on data dependencies.

questions.question: A 13B model in FP16 occupies 26 GB of weights on an 80 GB GPU, leaving 54 GB of free HBM. The model uses Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) with 40 layers, 8 KV heads, head dimension 128, and FP16 elements ($b=2$). For 64 concurrent requests at an 8,192-token context length, the required KV-cache memory is approximately 86 GB. What does this arithmetic demonstrate about serving capacity limits?
choices: KV cache scales linearly with sequence length and batch size, creating a second memory wall where serving capacity is capped by decode concurrency rather than model weight size
KV cache eliminates the need to load model weights on each decode step, making the decode phase compute-bound
KV cache must reside exclusively in CPU RAM, so the serving capacity is bound by PCIe transfer bandwidth rather than GPU HBM
KV cache consumes memory only during the prefill phase and is completely freed before the decode phase begins
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. KV cache scales linearly with sequence length and batch size, creating a second memory wall where serving capacity is capped by decode concurrency rather than model weight size. Per-token KV cache is $2 \times 2 \times n_{\text{layers}} \times n_{\text{kv\_heads}} \times d_{\text{head}} \times b = 4 \times 40 \times 8 \times 128 \times 2 = 327{,}680\text{ bytes} = 320\text{ KB/token}$. For 64 sequences of 8,192 tokens: $64 \times 8{,}192 \times 320\text{ KB} \approx 167.7\text{ GB}$ (or ~85.9 GB at mean sequence length 4,096), far exceeding the remaining 54 GB of GPU memory. Thus, even when model weights fit comfortably in single-device memory, KV-cache growth under realistic concurrency and context lengths becomes the binding capacity bottleneck. Decode still reloads weights every step (B), KV cache must reside in GPU HBM for bandwidth (C), and decode continuously expands KV state (D).
questions.learning_objective: Calculate KV-cache memory scaling and identify it as the binding capacity limit for concurrent LLM decode.

questions.question: Under contiguous KV-cache pre-allocation, serving engines reserve memory for each request's maximum potential context (e.g., 4,096 tokens), leading to 60–80% memory waste. How does PagedAttention eliminate this waste and multiply concurrent serving capacity?
choices: It reduces the arithmetic FLOPs of the attention mechanism by downsampling key and value vectors dynamically
It offloads all key and value tensors to host CPU RAM via zero-copy PCIe mapping
It maps logical sequence positions to non-contiguous fixed-size physical memory blocks on demand via a block table, eliminating internal and external fragmentation
It forces all concurrent sequences to share identical key-value matrices across layers
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. It maps logical sequence positions to non-contiguous fixed-size physical memory blocks on demand via a block table, eliminating internal and external fragmentation. PagedAttention adapts OS virtual memory paging to KV caches. Memory is divided into fixed-size physical blocks (pages, e.g., 16 tokens). Sequences allocate physical blocks only as new tokens are generated. A logical-to-physical block table tracks allocations, allowing logical tokens to reside in non-contiguous physical memory. When a sequence completes, its pages are immediately returned to the free pool. This eliminates internal fragmentation (unused reservations) and external fragmentation (unusable memory gaps), recovering the 60–80% wasted memory to support 2–4x higher concurrency. Arithmetic FLOPs remain unchanged (A), state stays on GPU (B), and unrelated requests keep independent KV data (D).
questions.learning_objective: Explain how PagedAttention's block-mapping architecture eliminates memory fragmentation to increase concurrent serving capacity.

questions.question: A production chatbot platform serves 10,000 concurrent user sessions that all share a common 2,000-token system prompt. Using the prefix caching mechanism, quantify the compute and memory savings and explain the resulting impact on Time-to-First-Token (TTFT).
questions.answer: Without prefix caching, every new session computes full prefill over the 2,000-token system prompt, consuming $10{,}000 \times 2{,}000 = 20{,}000{,}000$ tokens of redundant prefill matrix multiplications and allocating 20 million tokens of duplicate KV-cache memory. With prefix caching (e.g., using RadixTree block indexing), the 2,000-token prompt is processed through prefill exactly once and its KV blocks are shared read-only across all 10,000 sessions on that replica. This reduces KV memory for the system prompt by roughly $10{,}000\times$ (storing 1 copy instead of 10,000) and completely removes the 2,000-token prefill computation from the critical path of incoming requests. Time-to-First-Token (TTFT) drops by 80–95% (from seconds to tens of milliseconds) because the engine only needs to run prefill over the user's short query tail.
questions.learning_objective: Quantify compute and memory savings from prefix caching in shared-prompt workloads and evaluate its impact on Time-to-First-Token.

questions.question: When does speculative decoding provide a net speedup in production LLM serving, and under what conditions does it degrade throughput?
choices: It guarantees a strict $K\times$ latency speedup regardless of acceptance rate because verifying $K$ draft tokens in parallel consumes zero target-model compute

It provides net speedup when draft token acceptance rate $\alpha$ is high enough that parallel verification of $K$ tokens saves more target-model memory bandwidth than the added compute of the draft model; at low $\alpha$, verification overhead and wasted draft execution degrade performance
It is beneficial only when the target model is smaller than the draft model
It improves throughput only when all draft tokens are rejected, allowing the target model to generate new tokens from scratch
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. It provides net speedup when draft token acceptance rate $\alpha$ is high enough that parallel verification of $K$ tokens saves more target-model memory bandwidth than the added compute of the draft model; at low $\alpha$, verification overhead and wasted draft execution degrade performance. Speculative decoding runs a small, fast draft model to propose $K$ tokens autoregressively, then verifies all $K$ tokens in a single parallel target-model forward pass. Because the target model is memory-bandwidth-bound during decode, verifying $K$ tokens in one pass takes roughly the same time as generating 1 token. If acceptance rate $\alpha$ is high (e.g., >70%), the system generates $1 + \alpha K$ tokens per target step, achieving 2–3x speedup. However, if $\alpha$ is low (e.g., <30%), draft compute is wasted and target verification overhead adds latency without advancing tokens, resulting in net throughput slowdown.
questions.learning_objective: Evaluate the acceptance rate break-even threshold and performance trade-offs of speculative decoding in production serving.

questions.question: What sequence of operations governs one step of speculative decoding to ensure that the target model's exact output probability distribution is preserved losslessly?
choices: Target model generates $K$ candidate tokens in parallel -> Draft model verifies candidates sequentially -> Mismatched tokens are accepted unconditionally
Draft model and target model generate alternating tokens simultaneously without cross-model probability comparison
Draft model predicts all $K$ tokens -> Target model skips verification and appends candidates directly to the KV cache

Draft model autoregressively generates $K$ candidate tokens -> Target model executes a single parallel forward pass to compute verification probabilities for all $K$ candidates -> Target model accepts or rejects tokens sequentially up to the first mismatch and samples a corrected token from the residual distribution
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. Draft model autoregressively generates $K$ candidate tokens -> Target model executes a single parallel forward pass to compute verification probabilities for all $K$ candidates -> Target model accepts or rejects tokens sequentially up to the first mismatch and samples a corrected token from the residual distribution. Lossless speculative decoding guarantees that output distribution matches the target model exactly. The draft model first proposes $K$ tokens. The target model evaluates all $K$ candidate positions in one forward pass. The rejection sampling algorithm evaluates tokens sequentially: token $i$ is accepted with probability $\min(1, P_{\text{target}}(x_i)/P_{\text{draft}}(x_i))$. At the first rejection, the remaining draft tokens are discarded, and a replacement token is sampled from the adjusted distribution $\max(0, P_{\text{target}}(x) - P_{\text{draft}}(x))$. This guarantees mathematical equivalence to standard autoregressive sampling.
questions.learning_objective: Sequence the phases of speculative decoding and explain how rejection sampling preserves the target model's output distribution.

questions.question: Why does disaggregated serving separate the prefill phase and the decode phase into distinct, dedicated GPU hardware pools rather than co-locating both on the same accelerators?
choices: Prefill and decode share identical bottleneck profiles, but splitting them simplifies container deployment in Kubernetes

Prefill is compute-bound over large matrix multiplications while decode is memory-bandwidth-bound over weight streaming; splitting them allows each phase to run on hardware optimized for its specific bottleneck without mutual interference
Prefill generates activations that do not require KV caching, allowing prefill nodes to operate without GPU memory
Decode nodes do not require network connectivity to prefill nodes because KV cache is recomputed locally from scratch
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. Prefill is compute-bound over large matrix multiplications while decode is memory-bandwidth-bound over weight streaming; splitting them allows each phase to run on hardware optimized for its specific bottleneck without mutual interference. Prefill processes the entire input prompt in parallel (high arithmetic intensity, compute-bound, benefits from high-TFLOPS Tensor Cores). Decode generates one token at a time (arithmetic intensity $\approx 1$, memory-bandwidth-bound, benefits from high HBM bandwidth). In unified serving, long prefill bursts monopolize Tensor Cores and stall ongoing decode iterations, causing severe Time-to-Next-Token (ITL/TBT) latency spikes. Disaggregation isolates prefill onto compute-heavy nodes and decode onto bandwidth-heavy nodes, transferring the generated KV cache across high-speed interconnects (NVLink/InfiniBand) to maintain low P99 inter-token latency.
questions.learning_objective: Compare the hardware bottleneck profiles of prefill and decode phases to justify disaggregated serving architecture.

questions.question: A team plans to serve a 70B-parameter LLM in FP16 precision ($b=16$ bits). Using $\text{Memory}_{\text{weights}} = P \times (b/8)$ bytes, calculate the weight footprint, and determine the minimum sharding degree across 80 GB GPUs assuming KV cache and activation overhead require an additional 40 GB per replica.
choices: At least 3-way sharding (or 4-way in power-of-two configurations), because weights require $70 \times 10^9 \times 2 = 140\text{ GB}$ and total memory is $180\text{ GB}$, exceeding the capacity of two 80 GB GPUs ($160\text{ GB}$)
Single-GPU serving is sufficient because modern serving frameworks compress FP16 weights into GPU registers at runtime
At least 8-way sharding, because tensor parallelism is mathematically invalid on fewer than 8 GPUs
2-way sharding, because 140 GB of weights fits within two 80 GB GPUs ($160\text{ GB}$) by completely eliminating the KV cache
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. At least 3-way sharding (or 4-way in power-of-two configurations), because weights require $70 \times 10^9 \times 2 = 140\text{ GB}$ and total memory is $180\text{ GB}$, exceeding the capacity of two 80 GB GPUs ($160\text{ GB}$). Model weights in FP16 occupy $70 \times 10^9 \times 2\text{ bytes} = 140\text{ GB}$. Adding 40 GB for KV-cache state and runtime activation buffers yields a total memory requirement of $180\text{ GB}$. Two 80 GB GPUs provide only 160 GB total HBM, making 2-way sharding insufficient for production load. At minimum, 3 devices (240 GB) or standard 4-way/8-way tensor parallelism across NVLink is required. Weights cannot fit on one GPU without aggressive quantization (B), TP works on 2 or 4 GPUs (C), and eliminating KV cache prevents autoregressive generation (D).
questions.learning_objective: Apply the weight-memory formula and runtime overhead allowances to calculate the minimum sharding degree for large models.

questions.question: A service must optimize for the lowest possible single-request latency (Time-to-First-Token and Inter-Token Latency) under a strict P99 SLO. Which statement best contrasts tensor parallelism (TP) with pipeline parallelism (PP) for this objective?
choices: Pipeline parallelism reduces single-request latency more than tensor parallelism because inter-stage activation transfers require zero synchronization
Tensor parallelism is designed exclusively for recommendation systems while pipeline parallelism is designed for LLMs
Pipeline parallelism eliminates all inter-GPU communication by duplicating weights across all stages

Tensor parallelism reduces single-request latency by partitioning intra-layer matrix multiplications across GPUs with synchronous AllReduce collectives, whereas pipeline parallelism splits layers sequentially across stages and improves throughput via micro-batching without reducing single-request latency
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. Tensor parallelism reduces single-request latency by partitioning intra-layer matrix multiplications across GPUs with synchronous AllReduce collectives, whereas pipeline parallelism splits layers sequentially across stages and improves throughput via micro-batching without reducing single-request latency. In tensor parallelism (TP), each linear layer (attention QKV/out-proj and MLP) is sliced across $N$ GPUs (column/row parallel). All $N$ GPUs compute their partial GEMM simultaneously, dividing compute time by roughly $N$ at the cost of two AllReduce collectives per transformer block. In pipeline parallelism (PP), the model is partitioned depth-wise across $N$ stages. A single request must still traverse all $N$ stages sequentially, experiencing total compute time equal to or greater than single-GPU execution plus inter-stage communication latency. PP increases aggregate throughput by pipelining multiple micro-batches, not single-request latency.
questions.learning_objective: Compare tensor parallelism and pipeline parallelism mechanisms to evaluate their impact on single-request latency versus aggregate throughput.

questions.question: A 671B-parameter Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model routes each token to 8 out of 64 experts, activating only 37B parameters per token. Explain why per-token decode latency resembles a 37B dense model while hardware memory provisioning must accommodate the full 671B parameters, and describe the resulting sharding strategy.
questions.answer: During decode, memory bandwidth is consumed by streaming only the weights of the activated experts; because each token routes to top-8 experts totaling 37B parameters, the memory read volume per step is equivalent to a 37B dense model, delivering fast per-token decode latency. However, because token routing decisions are dynamic and data-dependent, any expert among the 671B total could be selected by incoming tokens; thus, the entire 671B parameter set (~1.34 TB in FP16) must remain resident in GPU cluster memory simultaneously. The resulting sharding strategy is expert parallelism (EP): expert sub-networks are partitioned across multiple GPUs (e.g., 8 to 64 GPUs), and an AllToAll collective routes token activations dynamically to the specific GPUs hosting the chosen experts.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze the capacity versus bandwidth divergence in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) inference and justify expert-parallel sharding.

questions.question: Which communication collective is the defining signature of expert parallelism for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) inference?
choices: AllReduce, because all GPUs compute identical tensor slices and sum the resulting scalar gradients
Broadcast, because the master GPU transmits the entire model parameter set to all worker GPUs on every token
AllToAll, because token representations must be dispatched dynamically to the GPUs hosting their chosen experts and the computed expert outputs must be gathered back to the originating GPUs
Point-to-point ring transfer, because tokens always visit expert GPUs in a fixed static numerical order
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. AllToAll, because token representations must be dispatched dynamically to the GPUs hosting their chosen experts and the computed expert outputs must be gathered back to the originating GPUs. In MoE layers, each token's gating router independently selects $k$ expert indices. Because experts are distributed across different GPUs, each device must send tokens destined for remote experts to their respective owner GPUs (AllToAll dispatch), and after expert FFN execution, collect the resulting activation tensors back to the originating tokens' GPUs (AllToAll gather). AllReduce (A) is used in tensor parallelism to sum partial matrix products. Broadcast (B) is for parameter synchronization, and static ring routing (D) cannot support data-dependent dynamic expert selection.
questions.learning_objective: Identify AllToAll collective communication as the defining data routing pattern in expert-parallel MoE serving.

questions.question: A recommendation platform operates 8 TB of sparse embedding tables across hundreds of categorical features, followed by a 15 GB dense ranking MLP. Which sharding strategy directly addresses the primary system bottleneck?
choices: Pipeline parallelism across the dense ranking MLP, because staged execution of dense layers is the primary latency constraint
Tensor parallelism across every embedding table lookup to replicate all tables on every GPU
Embedding table sharding (row-wise, column-wise, or table-wise) across host memory / SSD storage pools, because memory capacity and sparse lookup bandwidth are dominated by the embedding tables
Speculative decoding adapted to embedding retrieval to predict future user clicks autoregressively
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. Embedding table sharding (row-wise, column-wise, or table-wise) across host memory / SSD storage pools, because memory capacity and sparse lookup bandwidth are dominated by the embedding tables. In recommendation systems, 99% of model memory footprint (8 TB vs. 15 GB) resides in embedding tables. Sharding embedding tables across memory nodes—using table-wise partitioning (placing distinct tables on distinct nodes), row-wise partitioning (hashing embedding IDs across nodes), or column-wise partitioning (slicing embedding dimensions)—distributes both memory capacity and memory bus lookup bandwidth across the cluster. Sharding the 15 GB dense head (A) ignores the 8 TB bottleneck, replicating 8 TB on every GPU (B) is physically impossible, and speculative decoding (D) is an LLM generation technique.
questions.learning_objective: Select the appropriate sharding strategy for embedding-dominated recommendation systems based on memory and bandwidth bottlenecks.

questions.question: Under what condition does cross-node tensor parallelism over standard network fabrics (e.g., 200 Gbps Ethernet) cause a net latency slowdown compared to single-node execution?
choices: Whenever the number of GPUs $N$ is an odd number
When the model precision is converted from FP16 to FP8
When the serving engine uses continuous batching instead of static batching

When the cross-node AllReduce communication time $T_{\text{comm}}(N)$ exceeds the compute time saved by parallelizing matrix multiplications across $N$ devices: $T_{\text{comm}}(N) > T_{\text{compute}}(1 - 1/N)$
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. When the cross-node AllReduce communication time $T_{\text{comm}}(N)$ exceeds the compute time saved by parallelizing matrix multiplications across $N$ devices: $T_{\text{comm}}(N) > T_{\text{compute}}(1 - 1/N)$. In tensor parallelism, each transformer layer requires two synchronous AllReduce collectives directly in the critical execution path. Within a node, high-bandwidth NVLink (900 GB/s on H100) keeps $T_{\text{comm}}$ under tens of microseconds, making TP profitable. Across nodes over standard Ethernet/InfiniBand (25–50 GB/s), network latency and bandwidth limitations cause $T_{\text{comm}}$ to rise into milliseconds. If the communication overhead exceeds the compute reduction $(1 - 1/N)T_{\text{compute}}$, parallel execution takes longer than sequential execution, creating a net latency regression.
questions.learning_objective: Evaluate the communication-to-computation ratio to determine when interconnect bandwidth limits the viability of cross-node tensor parallelism.

questions.question: Why does the power-of-two-choices load balancing algorithm dramatically outperform uniform random routing in a large inference serving fleet?
choices: Sampling just two random replicas and dispatching to the one with the shorter queue reduces the maximum fleet queue length exponentially from $O(\ln N / \ln \ln N)$ to $O(\ln \ln N / \ln 2)$ with negligible probing overhead
It guarantees that all GPU replicas will have exactly zero queued requests at all times
It eliminates the need for network switches by routing packets directly between accelerators
It inspects every single server in the fleet before making each routing decision
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. Sampling just two random replicas and dispatching to the one with the shorter queue reduces the maximum fleet queue length exponentially from $O(\ln N / \ln \ln N)$ to $O(\ln \ln N / \ln 2)$ with negligible probing overhead. Under uniform random routing across $N$ servers, maximum queue length grows logarithmically with fleet size as $O(\ln N / \ln \ln N)$, creating severe queue hotspots that destroy P99 tail latency. By querying only $d=2$ random candidate replicas and assigning the request to the less-loaded one, the maximum queue length drops exponentially to $O(\ln \ln N / \ln 2)$—an essentially constant, flat queue depth even as $N$ scales to thousands of servers—without incurring the $O(N)$ probing overhead of querying every server.
questions.learning_objective: Explain the power-of-two-choices load balancing bound and its role in suppressing tail latency queue hotspots.

questions.question: Explain why least-connections routing is significantly more effective than round-robin routing for autoregressive LLM serving fleets, referencing request-duration variance.
questions.answer: Round-robin assumes that all requests impose equal processing cost and duration. In autoregressive LLM serving, output lengths vary by two orders of magnitude (e.g., a 30-token classification vs. a 3,000-token summarization, representing a 100x variance in execution duration). Under round-robin, an unlucky replica can be assigned multiple long-running requests in succession, saturating its KV-cache memory and decode slots while neighboring replicas sit idle. Least-connections routing dynamically tracks the number of active in-flight requests per replica and assigns incoming traffic to the replica with the fewest active connections, naturally balancing the cumulative execution load and preventing hotspot-induced queueing delays.
questions.learning_objective: Justify least-connections routing over round-robin for serving workloads with high output duration variance.

questions.question: A multi-turn conversational LLM service routes requests across 50 GPU replicas. Why is consistent hashing (e.g., hashing session/user ID to a virtual node ring) superior to standard modulo hashing ($h(\text{ID}) \pmod N$) for session affinity?
choices: Consistent hashing compresses the KV cache by 50% across all nodes on the ring

When a replica fails or an autoscaling event adds a node, consistent hashing remaps only $1/N$ of active sessions, preserving KV-cache locality for the remaining $(N-1)/N$ sessions, whereas modulo hashing remaps virtually 100% of sessions
Consistent hashing eliminates the need for GPU memory by storing conversation tokens in the hash table
Modulo hashing is incompatible with IPv6 network protocols
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. When a replica fails or an autoscaling event adds a node, consistent hashing remaps only $1/N$ of active sessions, preserving KV-cache locality for the remaining $(N-1)/N$ sessions, whereas modulo hashing remaps virtually 100% of sessions. In stateful LLM serving, preserving KV-cache session affinity avoids the expensive prefill recomputation of conversation history. Under standard modulo hashing, changing fleet size from $N$ to $N+1$ alters the modulus $h \pmod{N+1}$ for almost every key, invalidating cached KV state across the entire fleet and triggering a storm of redundant prefill computation. Consistent hashing maps servers and session IDs onto a continuous virtual ring, ensuring that scaling events disrupt only the fraction $1/N$ of keys immediately adjacent on the ring.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze how consistent hashing preserves KV-cache session affinity during fleet scaling and node failure events.

questions.question: What is the primary operational role of a circuit breaker in an inference serving cluster?
choices: It physically cuts power to the data center rack whenever GPU temperature exceeds 80 degrees Celsius
It dynamically converts floating-point weights into integers during high-load periods
It re-routes all incoming user requests to the training cluster when serving GPUs are full

It rapidly isolates degraded or thermally throttled GPU replicas when their error or latency thresholds are breached, failing fast and preventing client retry storms from causing fleet-wide cascading collapse
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. It rapidly isolates degraded or thermally throttled GPU replicas when their error or latency thresholds are breached, failing fast and preventing client retry storms from causing fleet-wide cascading collapse. When a GPU replica degrades (e.g., PCIe errors, thermal throttling, or memory thrashing), its response latency spikes from 50 ms to seconds. Without a circuit breaker, the load balancer continues routing requests to the slow server; queued requests time out, triggering client retries that multiply traffic and overwhelm healthy replicas, leading to a cascading failure. A circuit breaker tracks error/latency rates per replica and trips open when thresholds are breached, instantly shedding traffic from the unhealthy instance and allowing the rest of the fleet to maintain normal SLO compliance.
questions.learning_objective: Describe how circuit breakers isolate degraded inference replicas to prevent cascading fleet failures.

questions.question: A serving fleet comprises 10 H100 servers (delivering 2,000 tokens/sec each) and 20 A100 servers (delivering 1,000 tokens/sec each). How should a capacity-weighted load balancer distribute incoming traffic to maximize throughput while preventing server overload?
choices: Route 100% of traffic to the H100 servers until they reach 100% capacity, then spill excess traffic to the A100 servers

Assign traffic in a 2:1 ratio (weight 2 for each H100, weight 1 for each A100), allocating 50% of total traffic to the H100 pool and 50% to the A100 pool so all servers operate at equal relative utilization
Distribute traffic equally with 1:1 weighting across all 30 servers regardless of hardware generation
Route all short requests to A100 servers and all long requests to H100 servers without capacity weighting
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. Assign traffic in a 2:1 ratio (weight 2 for each H100, weight 1 for each A100), allocating 50% of total traffic to the H100 pool and 50% to the A100 pool so all servers operate at equal relative utilization. Aggregate fleet capacity is $(10 \times 2{,}000) + (20 \times 1{,}000) = 20{,}000 + 20{,}000 = 40{,}000\text{ tokens/sec}$. With 2:1 weighting, each H100 receives twice the request volume of an A100. The 10 H100s process $20{,}000/40{,}000 = 50\%$ of traffic, and the 20 A100s process the other $50\%$, matching their respective physical throughput capacities. Equal weighting (C) would overload the A100s at 150% capacity while leaving H100s at 75% utilization, causing severe queueing and SLO violations on the A100 pool.
questions.learning_objective: Calculate capacity-weighted traffic distribution for heterogeneous accelerator serving clusters to balance relative utilization.

questions.question: In a shared multi-tenant inference platform hosting Tenants A, B, and C on a common GPU pool, Tenant A suddenly launches a burst of long-context summarization requests that consume 75% of the shared KV-cache memory pool. What does the noisy-neighbor phenomenon predict will happen to Tenants B and C?
choices: Tenants B and C experience improved latency because statistical multiplexing automatically smooths out burst traffic without explicit isolation
Multi-tenancy guarantees hardware isolation automatically through GPU kernel multi-threading without software quotas
Tenants B and C experience severe P99 latency degradation and reduced concurrency because shared KV-cache memory, HBM bandwidth, and compute slots are contested resources consumed by Tenant A's burst
Tenants B and C are unaffected because KV cache memory is allocated exclusively from host CPU RAM
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. Tenants B and C experience severe P99 latency degradation and reduced concurrency because shared KV-cache memory, HBM bandwidth, and compute slots are contested resources consumed by Tenant A's burst. In shared GPU inference, unpartitioned memory pools allow a single tenant's long-context or high-QPS surge to allocate disproportionate KV-cache blocks. As available memory shrinks, the serving engine is forced to reduce batch sizes or evict pages for co-located tenants, dropping their concurrency and creating queueing backlogs. Shared HBM bandwidth and Tensor Core execution time are also contested, degrading P99 latency across all tenants unless strict isolation controls (quotas, bulkheads) are enforced.
questions.learning_objective: Identify the mechanisms of noisy-neighbor performance degradation in shared multi-tenant GPU inference clusters.

questions.question: Compare the utilization-versus-isolation trade-offs between hard resource quotas and soft quotas with fair sharing in a multi-tenant inference platform, and identify the scenario where hard quotas remain necessary.
questions.answer: Hard quotas enforce fixed, immutable capacity ceilings (e.g., max concurrent tokens/sec) on each tenant. They guarantee deterministic performance isolation and prevent any noisy-neighbor interference, but cause substantial resource underutilization when tenants are idle, leaving expensive GPUs unused. Soft quotas with fair sharing (e.g., max-min fairness) allow tenants to burst above their baseline allocations when the cluster is underutilized (e.g., 50% load), but dynamically throttle them back to their fair share as total cluster demand approaches saturation (e.g., 90% load). This maximizes fleet utilization and cost efficiency while preserving isolation under contention. Hard quotas remain strictly necessary for high-value contractual SLAs (e.g., Enterprise tiers with legally binding P99 latency guarantees) and safety-critical workloads where zero interference must be provably guaranteed.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze the trade-offs between hard quotas and soft fair-share quotas in multi-tenant serving platforms.

questions.question: How does priority scheduling with preemption handle an incoming high-priority Critical request when all GPU batch slots are currently occupied by lower-priority Best-Effort requests?
choices: The scheduler selects a Best-Effort request as a victim, swaps its accumulated KV cache to CPU host memory (or checkpoints its state), and immediately assigns the freed GPU slot to the Critical request
The Critical request is rejected immediately with a 503 Service Unavailable error
The scheduler waits indefinitely for all Best-Effort requests to finish their complete generations naturally under FCFS order
The scheduler terminates all running Best-Effort processes permanently and reboots the GPU instance
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. The scheduler selects a Best-Effort request as a victim, swaps its accumulated KV cache to CPU host memory (or checkpoints its state), and immediately assigns the freed GPU slot to the Critical request. In priority-aware serving, Critical traffic must never wait behind background batch jobs. When GPU compute and KV slots are saturated, preemption suspends an active lower-priority generation, saves its KV cache state to host CPU RAM, and yields the accelerator resources to the Critical request. Once the high-priority work finishes, the preempted job's KV cache is restored from CPU memory to resume generation from its last token rather than restarting from scratch.
questions.learning_objective: Explain how priority scheduling and KV-cache preemption preserve latency SLOs for critical inference traffic.

questions.question: Which statement best distinguishes deployment-level bulkheads from request-level bulkheads in multi-tenant inference architectures?
choices: Deployment-level bulkheads physically isolate tenant tiers onto dedicated GPU replica pools to prevent cascading cluster failures, whereas request-level bulkheads enforce bounds on individual request size (max input/output tokens, execution timeouts) within shared processes
Deployment-level bulkheads operate inside GPU CUDA kernels, whereas request-level bulkheads manage DNS records
Request-level bulkheads provide complete physical hardware isolation, whereas deployment-level bulkheads rely on software quotas
Deployment-level bulkheads eliminate all operational hosting costs by sharing GPUs with external cloud tenants
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. Deployment-level bulkheads physically isolate tenant tiers onto dedicated GPU replica pools to prevent cascading cluster failures, whereas request-level bulkheads enforce bounds on individual request size (max input/output tokens, execution timeouts) within shared processes. Analogous to watertight ship compartments, deployment-level bulkheads partition infrastructure physically: critical Enterprise tenants run on dedicated GPU pools unaffected by traffic spikes or crashes in the Standard/Free tiers. Request-level bulkheads operate within shared services to prevent individual pathological requests (e.g., a query requesting 32,000 output tokens) from monopolizing compute slots or crashing workers with out-of-memory errors.
questions.learning_objective: Contrast deployment-level and request-level bulkhead isolation patterns and their roles in fault containment.

questions.question: The scaling response time budget is defined as $T_{\text{response}} = T_{\text{detect}} + T_{\text{decide}} + T_{\text{provision}} + T_{\text{warmup}}$. In cold-starting a 70B LLM replica on an H100 instance, which component dominates the multi-minute startup lag, and how do tiered warm pools remediate it?
choices: $T_{\text{detect}}$ dominates because metrics collection takes 15 minutes
$T_{\text{decide}}$ dominates because the autoscaling algorithm takes 10 minutes to solve an optimization problem

$T_{\text{provision}}$ and $T_{\text{load}}$ dominate (5–7 minutes downloading 140 GB of model weights from object storage and loading to GPU); warm pools keep pre-warmed replicas in Hot (instant) or Warm (30s) readiness states to absorb spikes without cold-start delay
$T_{\text{warmup}}$ dominates because GPU warming requires re-training the first transformer layer
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. $T_{\text{provision}}$ and $T_{\text{load}}$ dominate (5–7 minutes downloading 140 GB of model weights from object storage and loading to GPU); warm pools keep pre-warmed replicas in Hot (instant) or Warm (30s) readiness states to absorb spikes without cold-start delay. Cold starts for large models are dominated by VM provisioning and transferring tens of gigabytes of weights over the network ($T_{\text{provision}} + T_{\text{load}} \approx 3\text{--}7\text{ min}$), causing reactive autoscaling to fail during sudden surges. Tiered warm pools trade cost for readiness: Hot replicas (GPU allocated, model running) absorb bursts instantly at 100% cost; Warm replicas (GPU allocated, weights loaded) activate in ~30s at ~60% cost; Cold replicas cost 0% but require 5+ minutes.
questions.learning_objective: Decompose GPU scaling response time and evaluate how tiered warm pools eliminate cold-start latency spikes.

questions.question: A team deploys a single-region LLM service in US-East. Interactive users in Tokyo experience an inescapable network Round-Trip Time (RTT) of ~150 ms before model execution begins. What does the global inference architecture framework prescribe for this deployment?
choices: Deploy cross-region pipeline parallelism with early layers in US-East and later layers in Tokyo to eliminate network latency
Deploy independent regional inference replicas in Asia-Pacific to reduce network RTT to <10 ms, complemented by edge caching for high-repeatability queries (e.g., FAQ/autocomplete)
Increase GPU memory on US-East servers to accelerate light speed across transpacific fiber cables
Use round-robin DNS to force Tokyo users to connect exclusively through European data centers
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. Deploy independent regional inference replicas in Asia-Pacific to reduce network RTT to <10 ms, complemented by edge caching for high-repeatability queries (e.g., FAQ/autocomplete). Fundamental physics limits speed-of-light transoceanic RTT (150–200 ms from Tokyo/Sydney to US-East). For interactive multi-turn applications, this network floor compounds on every user interaction. Replicating models regionally reduces RTT to local levels (<10 ms). Edge caching on CDN PoPs returns repeated queries (autocomplete hit rate 60–80%, FAQ 40–60%) in <10 ms without backend model execution. Cross-region pipeline parallelism (A) is a disastrous anti-pattern because 150 ms inter-stage latency dwarfs 2 ms per-layer compute.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze the network RTT latency floor in global inference and select the appropriate regional replication and edge caching patterns.

AWQ (Activation-aware Weight Quantization) salient channel protection

questions.question: Why do production LLMs (e.g., Llama, GPT architectures) suffer catastrophic perplexity degradation under naive round-to-nearest Post-Training Quantization (PTQ), necessitating specialized methods such as AWQ and SmoothQuant?
choices: Model weights in LLMs are inherently non-differentiable after training
Integer arithmetic is physically incompatible with transformer attention softmax layers
Quantization increases model weight memory footprint on GPU HBM

A tiny fraction (~0.1%) of activation channels exhibit extreme numerical outliers (up to 100x larger than median values), which collapse the dynamic range and cause massive truncation error when quantized with per-tensor scales
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. A tiny fraction (~0.1%) of activation channels exhibit extreme numerical outliers (up to 100x larger than median values), which collapse the dynamic range and cause massive truncation error when quantized with per-tensor scales. Research in LLM quantization reveals that starting around 6B+ parameters, transformer activations develop systematic outlier channels across specific feature dimensions with magnitudes 10–100x larger than normal activations. In naive uniform quantization, scaling factors are forced to accommodate these massive outliers, reducing the effective precision of the remaining 99.9% of normal channels to near zero. Specialized methods resolve this: AWQ protects the top 1% salient weight channels corresponding to high-magnitude activations, while SmoothQuant mathematically migrates the scaling challenge from activations to weights.
questions.learning_objective: Identify the activation outlier phenomenon as the root cause of naive PTQ degradation in large language models.

questions.question: What is the core algorithmic mechanism of Activation-Aware Weight Quantization (AWQ)?
choices: It retrains the entire model using backpropagation and Adam optimizer on 100 billion tokens

It uses a small calibration dataset to observe activation magnitudes, identifies the top 1% of salient weight channels corresponding to large activations, and protects them by keeping them in higher precision or scaling them to minimize output error
It removes all activation functions (ReLU, GELU, SwiGLU) from the transformer architecture
It quantizes all weights to 1-bit binary representations using stochastic gradient descent
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. It uses a small calibration dataset to observe activation magnitudes, identifies the top 1% of salient weight channels corresponding to large activations, and protects them by keeping them in higher precision or scaling them to minimize output error. AWQ observes that not all weights in an LLM are equally important: weights that interact with high-magnitude activation channels have a disproportionate impact on output error. Rather than quantizing all weights uniformly, AWQ profiles a small calibration set (e.g., 128 sequences), measures per-channel activation magnitude $s_X$, and protects the top ~1% most salient weight channels. It optimizes a per-channel scale factor that protects salient weights without requiring expensive activation quantization or full model retraining (QAT).
questions.learning_objective: Explain the salient weight protection mechanism in Activation-Aware Weight Quantization (AWQ).

questions.question: A 70B-parameter LLM quantized from FP16 (140 GB) to INT4 (35 GB) is deployed for autoregressive decoding on an H100 GPU (3.35 TB/s HBM bandwidth). Explain the physical mechanism by which this quantization delivers an approximate 4x throughput speedup during the decode phase.
questions.answer: During autoregressive decoding (batch size 1 or small batches), the GPU is memory-bandwidth-bound on reading model weights from HBM to on-chip SRAM for each generated token ($T_{\text{step}} \approx \text{Memory}_{\text{weights}} / \text{Bandwidth}_{\text{HBM}}$). In FP16, streaming 140 GB of weights requires $140\text{ GB} / 3{,}350\text{ GB/s} \approx 41.8\text{ ms/token}$, capping maximum decode throughput at ~24 tokens/sec. In INT4 (4 bits per weight), the weight footprint shrinks to 35 GB, requiring only $35\text{ GB} / 3{,}350\text{ GB/s} \approx 10.4\text{ ms/token}$ to stream, accelerating decode throughput by roughly $4\times$ to ~96 tokens/sec. Furthermore, the 35 GB footprint allows the full 70B model to fit within a single 80 GB GPU, eliminating multi-GPU tensor parallelism and its associated AllReduce communication overhead.
questions.learning_objective: Calculate the memory-bandwidth decode speedup achieved by weight quantization and explain the single-device consolidation dividend.

questions.question: How does SmoothQuant enable efficient 8-bit weight and 8-bit activation (W8A8) matrix multiplication on standard integer Tensor Cores without custom matrix kernels?
choices: It applies a per-channel smoothing scale factor $s$ to divide activations and multiply weights ($Y = (X \cdot \text{diag}(s)^{-1}) \cdot (\text{diag}(s) \cdot W)$), migrating outlier difficulty from activations to weights where both can be quantized uniformly
It deletes outlier activation values and replaces them with zeros at runtime
It executes activations in FP32 on CPU while streaming weights in INT8 on GPU
It runs forward inference backward in time to cancel out quantization noise
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. It applies a per-channel smoothing scale factor $s$ to divide activations and multiply weights ($Y = (X \cdot \text{diag}(s)^{-1}) \cdot (\text{diag}(s) \cdot W)$), migrating outlier difficulty from activations to weights where both can be quantized uniformly. SmoothQuant exploits the mathematical equivalence $Y = XW = (X \cdot \text{diag}(s)^{-1}) \cdot (\text{diag}(s) \cdot W) = \hat{X}\hat{W}$. Because activation outliers are concentrated in a few persistent channels across tokens, SmoothQuant computes a per-channel scale $s_j = \max(|X_j|)^\alpha / \max(|W_j|)^{1-\alpha}$ (where $\alpha \approx 0.5$). Dividing activation channels by $s$ squashes activation spikes into a quantizable dynamic range, while multiplying corresponding weight columns by $s$ is easily absorbed by weights. Both $\hat{X}$ and $\hat{W}$ can then be quantized with standard INT8 scales and computed on native INT8 Tensor Cores.
questions.learning_objective: Explain the mathematically equivalent scale migration mechanism of SmoothQuant for W8A8 deployment.

questions.question: When serving LLMs on modern GPU architectures with native FP8 Tensor Core support (e.g., NVIDIA Hopper), what is the key systems trade-off between native FP8 (E4M3) execution and weight-only INT4 (W4A16) execution?
choices: Native FP8 consumes 4x more HBM bandwidth than FP16
W4A16 can only be executed on CPUs and cannot run on GPU accelerators
FP8 causes total model accuracy collapse on all models above 1 billion parameters

Native FP8 accelerates both memory bandwidth and arithmetic compute throughput (2x FP16 TFLOPS) without runtime dequantization overhead, whereas W4A16 maximizes memory bandwidth savings (4x footprint reduction) but requires runtime dequantization from INT4 to FP16 before computation
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. Native FP8 accelerates both memory bandwidth and arithmetic compute throughput (2x FP16 TFLOPS) without runtime dequantization overhead, whereas W4A16 maximizes memory bandwidth savings (4x footprint reduction) but requires runtime dequantization from INT4 to FP16 before computation. Native FP8 (e.g., E4M3) is directly supported by Tensor Core hardware: activations and weights remain in FP8, doubling arithmetic matrix multiply throughput (TFLOPS) while halving memory footprint and bandwidth compared to FP16. In contrast, weight-only INT4 (W4A16) stores weights in 4 bits (4x footprint reduction, optimal for memory-bound decode at small batches), but requires a fused GPU kernel to dequantize INT4 weights back to FP16 registers on the fly, performing compute in FP16 and providing zero speedup for compute-bound prefill passes.
questions.learning_objective: Compare native FP8 hardware execution with weight-only INT4 runtime dequantization across compute and memory dimensions.

questions.question: Which production case study most directly exemplifies feature-parallel batching, multi-terabyte embedding table sharding across hybrid CPU/SSD storage pools, and GPU-accelerated dense interaction ranking?
choices: OpenAI's ChatGPT interactive text generation infrastructure
Autonomous vehicle onboard perception pipelines running on embedded edge accelerators
Meta's Deep Learning Recommendation Model (DLRM) serving architecture at hyper-scale
Google's real-time speech-to-text streaming pipeline
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. Meta's Deep Learning Recommendation Model (DLRM) serving architecture at hyper-scale. Meta's production recommendation infrastructure represents the canonical feature-parallel, embedding-dominated workload. Models contain multi-terabyte embedding tables that cannot fit in GPU HBM, requiring distributed sharding across host DRAM and high-speed NVMe SSD pools. Requests are routed feature-parallel across shards to fetch sparse representations, which are aggregated and dispatched to GPU workers for dense neural network interaction ranking. In contrast, OpenAI (A) serves autoregressive LLMs with continuous batching and KV caching, autonomous vehicles (B) process streaming sensor frames, and speech systems (D) process audio streaming frames.

questions.question: Compare why OpenAI's serving infrastructure centers on continuous batching, paged KV-cache memory, and stateful session routing, whereas Meta's recommendation infrastructure centers on distributed embedding sharding and feature-parallel routing.
questions.answer: The two architectures diverge because their binding physical bottlenecks are fundamentally different. OpenAI serves autoregressive LLMs where generation is iterative and sequence lengths vary widely; the primary bottlenecks are GPU memory capacity (holding dynamic KV caches) and memory bandwidth (streaming weights per token). Hence, OpenAI optimizes with continuous batching (iteration-level scheduling), paged KV caches (PagedAttention), and stateful sticky routing to preserve session KV context. In contrast, Meta's recommendation models process non-autoregressive, fixed-step queries dominated by multi-terabyte sparse embedding tables; the primary bottleneck is memory capacity and random memory lookup bandwidth across petabytes of categorical IDs. Hence, Meta optimizes with distributed embedding table sharding across host RAM/SSDs and feature-parallel lookup routing, feeding dense representations to GPU ranking MLPs.
questions.learning_objective: Contrast the bottleneck profiles and serving architectures of OpenAI's LLM platform and Meta's DLRM recommendation platform.

questions.question: What cross-cutting architectural principle is demonstrated by comparing production deployments across OpenAI, Meta, Google, and Autonomous Vehicles?

Recommendation systems and large language models share identical memory access patterns and run efficiently on identical serving stacks

Production inference systems reject one-size-fits-all designs: serving architecture must be strictly customized to the workload's specific bottleneck profile (memory capacity, weight bandwidth, sparse lookup, or hard real-time latency)
Edge inference deployments can execute identical containerized cloud serving stacks without adaptation
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. Production inference systems reject one-size-fits-all designs: serving architecture must be strictly customized to the workload's specific bottleneck profile (memory capacity, weight bandwidth, sparse lookup, or hard real-time latency). The case studies collectively prove that no single serving architecture is universally optimal. Workloads with sparse memory bottlenecks (DLRM) require CPU/SSD sharding and feature parallelism; autoregressive token generation (ChatGPT) requires continuous batching, paged KV caches, and stateful routing; search retrieval requires multi-tier edge caching; and autonomous vehicles require hard real-time single-frame streaming with zero accumulation delay. Attempting to deploy a generic stack across all workloads guarantees severe latency, cost, or capacity failures.
